---
title: "Research"
---

**I study how children and adolescents regulate emotion within family and peer
systems, and how moment-to-moment regulatory dynamics become longer-term
patterns of adaptation and physiological health.**

Four areas organise the work. They are not separate projects so much as four
views of one question: regulation is dynamic, it is physiological, it is
learned in relationships, and it accumulates into health.

## Biopsychosocial self-regulation

Regulation is not a trait and not a single strategy. Within one frustrating
episode a preschooler will try several things in sequence, distracting, seeking
help, then venting, while their parasympathetic activity shifts underneath.
Measuring regulation *statically*, as a questionnaire score or a single observed
strategy, has held the field back.

My work measures it as it unfolds: **polyregulation** (how strategies combine),
**temporal variation in respiratory sinus arrhythmia** across an episode, and
the correspondence between the two.

::: {.diagram}

Anchor papers: polyregulation in *Child Development* (2026); temporal variation
in RSA in *Infant and Child Development* (2025).

## Stress, adaptation, and resilience

Social stressors such as discrimination, socioeconomic risk, and academic
adversity affect health through pathways that are visible in daily life before
they are visible in disease. My work traces that route: from a stressor
reported today, through the *shape* of a person's affect (how sticky it is, how
variable), into physiological load, and eventually into health.

Resilience enters as a moderator rather than an outcome. The same stressor does
not produce the same affective signature in everyone, and in high-adversity
contexts some patterns we habitually call maladaptive appear to function
protectively.

::: {.diagram}

<figcaption>Stressors do not act on health directly. They act on the shape of
daily affect, which registers physiologically, which accumulates. Each arrow is
measurable at a different timescale, which is why intensive longitudinal designs
matter here.</figcaption>
:::

## Family and intergenerational dynamics

Regulation is learned somewhere. In Chinese three-generation households it is
co-performed: grandmother, mother, and child regulate together, sometimes in
physiological lockstep. I have shown grandmother and grandchild RSA synchrony in
these families, and traced how congruence between a child's attachment to two
different caregivers relates to what the child can do alone.

::: {.diagram}

Anchor papers: grandmother and grandchild synchrony in *Developmental

## Peer relations and friendship development

My dissertation moves this question into the peer world. Adolescents sit in
friendship structures that differ not just in *how many* friends they have but
in how those friendships are organised, including how diverse their cliques are,
how stable, and how overlapping. I ask whether that structure predicts
physiological wear-and-tear, and whether friends who cope similarly amplify or
buffer each other.

::: {.diagram}
